content: 1. A randomized clinical trial conducted in Botswana evaluated the two-year outcomes of antiretroviral therapy regimens containing zidovudine and didanosine in adults infected with HIV-1 subtype C. The study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2009. 2. A study assessed the evolution of drug resistance over 48 weeks in patients receiving zidovudine, lamivudine, and tenofovir without real-time viral load monitoring. The findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2010. 3. Research conducted in rural northwestern Uganda identified risk factors for virological failure and subtherapeutic antiretroviral drug concentrations in HIV-positive adults. This study was published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2009. 4. An effectiveness assessment of scaling up highly active antiretroviral therapy in a rural district of Malawi demonstrated positive outcomes. The results were published in The Lancet in 2006. 5. A study in Angola used dried blood spots to evaluate subtype variability, virological response, and drug resistance in HIV patients on antiretroviral therapy. The findings were published in the Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in 2008. 6. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection provide comprehensive recommendations for clinical practice. 7. A study in Cameroon found low levels of antiretroviral-resistant HIV infections in a routine clinic setting using the WHO public health approach. The results were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2009. 8. A randomized controlled study (MiniZID) evaluated the safety of zidovudine dose reduction in treatment-naive HIV-infected patients. The findings were published in HIV Medicine in 2016. 9. Research demonstrated that tenofovir renal toxicity specifically targets the mitochondria of renal proximal tubules. This study was published in Laboratory Investigation in 2009. 10. A study highlighted the association between tenofovir use and bone density loss. The findings were published in Therapeutics and Clinical Risk Management in 2010. 11. A 96-week analysis compared tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, emtricitabine, and efavirenz with fixed-dose zidovudine/lamivudine and efavirenz in antiretroviral-naive patients, focusing on virological, immunological, and morphological changes. The results were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2006. 12. Long-term renal safety of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in antiretroviral-naive HIV-1-infected patients was evaluated in a double-blind, randomized, active-controlled multicenter study. The findings were published in Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation in 2005. 13. A three-year randomized trial compared the efficacy and safety of tenofovir DF versus stavudine in combination therapy for antiretroviral-naive patients. The results were published in JAMA in 2004. 14. A systematic review by WHO assessed adverse reactions associated with tenofovir and integrase inhibitors to inform consolidated antiretroviral therapy guidelines. 15. A phase 2 study compared tenofovir alafenamide with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in single-tablet regimens for initial HIV-1 therapy. The findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2014. 16. Two phase 3 trials compared tenofovir alafenamide and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate coformulated with elvitegravir, cobicistat, and emtricitabine for initial HIV-1 treatment. The results were published in The Lancet in 2015. 17. A study demonstrated a high rate of reversibility of renal damage in HIV-infected patients receiving tenofovir-containing antiretroviral therapy. The findings were published in Antiviral Research in 2012. 18. Research linked tenofovir exposure to an increased risk of kidney disease in HIV-infected patients. The study was published in AIDS in 2012. 19. A study evaluated the recovery rate of renal function in HIV-infected patients who discontinued tenofovir treatment. The findings were published in HIV Medicine in 2014. 20. Renal impairment in HIV-infected patients initiating tenofovir-containing antiretroviral therapy in a primary healthcare setting in South Africa was investigated. The results were published in Tropical Medicine & International Health in 2015. 21. A systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the renal safety of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in HIV-infected patients. The findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2010. 22. An update on tenofovir nephrotoxicity was provided in a study published in AIDS Research and Treatment in 2011. 23. A study examined renal function in HIV patients starting therapy with tenofovir and either efavirenz, lopinavir, or atazanavir. The findings were published in AIDS in 2012. 24. A systematic review evaluated the accuracy of urine glucose dipstick testing for detecting renal toxicity in HIV-infected patients taking tenofovir. 25. A cross-sectional study found a strong correlation between protein reagent strip results and protein-to-creatinine ratios for detecting renal dysfunction in HIV-infected patients. The findings were published in AIDS Research and Therapy in 2015. 26. WHO guidelines assessed the accuracy of glycosuria or proteinuria/albuminuria dipsticks for screening and monitoring tenofovir-associated tubulopathy in resource-limited settings. 27. A phase 2b trial evaluated once-daily dolutegravir in combination therapy for antiretroviral-naive adults with HIV. The interim 48-week results were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2012. 28. A randomized, double-blind, non-inferiority study compared once-daily dolutegravir with raltegravir in antiretroviral-naive adults with HIV-1 infection. The 48-week results were published in The Lancet in 2013. 29. The VIKING study evaluated the safety and efficacy of dolutegravir in treatment-experienced subjects with raltegravir-resistant HIV-1 infection. The 24-week results were published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2013. 30. A phase 1 study assessed dolutegravir's effect on renal function using iohexol and para-aminohippurate clearance measurements in healthy subjects. The findings were published in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology in 2012. 31. A review summarized the clinical pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and drug-interaction profile of the integrase inhibitor dolutegravir. The findings were published in Clinical Pharmacokinetics in 2013. 32. The BENCHMRK studies reported the efficacy and safety of raltegravir for HIV treatment over five years. The final results were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2013. 33. The ANRS 12180 Reflate TB study evaluated raltegravir for treating patients co-infected with HIV and tuberculosis. The results were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2014. 34. A study from the D:A:D cohort collaboration investigated the use of nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors and the risk of myocardial infarction in HIV-infected patients. The findings were published in The Lancet in 2008. 35. A review discussed the use of nucleoside and nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors in children. The findings were published in Clinical Drug Investigation in 2007. 36. The PREDICT-1 study demonstrated the utility of HLA-B5701 screening for preventing hypersensitivity to abacavir. The findings were published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2008. 37. A systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed the association between HLA-B5701 genotypes and abacavir-induced hypersensitivity reactions. The findings were published in the Journal of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences in 2015. 38. The PENTA 5 trial compared dual nucleoside-analogue reverse-transcriptase inhibitor regimens with and without nelfinavir in children with HIV-1. The results were published in The Lancet in 2002. 39. A randomized, double-blind study compared triple nucleoside therapy with abacavir, lamivudine, and zidovudine versus lamivudine and zidovudine in previously treated HIV-1-infected children. The findings were published in Pediatrics in 2001. 40. A systematic review evaluated the safety of efavirenz during the first trimester of pregnancy. The findings were included in the WHO consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use. 41. The Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry Steering Committee reported on the safety of antiretroviral drugs during pregnancy, including data from 1989 to 2015. 42. A study presented at the 21st Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI) in 2014 linked maternal tenofovir use to lower newborn bone mineral content. 43. Research evaluated the safety of tenofovir use during pregnancy and its impact on early growth outcomes in HIV-exposed uninfected infants. The findings were published in AIDS in 2012. 44. A study investigated the pharmacokinetics of the HIV integrase inhibitor S/GSK1349572 when co-administered with acid-reducing agents and multivitamins in healthy volunteers. The findings were published in the Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in 2011. 45. Neonatal mortality in HIV-exposed infants born to women receiving combination antiretroviral therapy in rural Uganda was studied. The findings were published in the Journal of Tropical Pediatrics in 2013. 46. A study in Botswana examined the association between highly active antiretroviral therapy and adverse birth outcomes among HIV-infected women. The findings were published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2012. 47. Research evaluated the risk of preterm delivery in women initiating antiretroviral therapy to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV. The findings were published in HIV Medicine in 2014. 48. A study investigated the role of ritonavir boosting in premature delivery among HIV-infected women starting protease inhibitor therapy during pregnancy. The findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2012. 49. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the timing of antiretroviral therapy initiation and its association with adverse pregnancy outcomes. 50. The PROMISE study confirmed WHO recommendations to treat pregnant women and reduce mother-to-child transmission of HIV. 51. WHO guidelines for the treatment of tuberculosis and drug-resistant tuberculosis provide comprehensive recommendations for clinical management. 52. A review discussed the challenges of treating hepatitis C virus infection with direct-acting antiviral drugs in HIV-positive patients. The findings were published in Current Opinion in Infectious Diseases in 2013. 53. A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the impact of direct-acting antivirals on hepatitis C in HIV-infected patients. The findings were published in Drugs in 2014. 54. WHO guidelines for the treatment of malaria provide evidence-based recommendations for clinical practice. 55. WHO guidelines for the psychosocially assisted pharmacological treatment of opioid dependence offer comprehensive recommendations for clinical management. 56. WHO's medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use provide evidence-based guidance for family planning in various clinical scenarios. 57. A review discussed drug interactions between antiretrovirals and hormonal contraceptives. The findings were published in Expert Opinion on Drug Metabolism & Toxicology in 2013. 58. WHO's package of essential noncommunicable disease interventions for primary healthcare in low-resource settings provides practical guidance for clinical management. 59. A review summarized recent literature on antiretroviral regimens sparing agents from the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor class. The findings were published in AIDS Research and Therapy.
